statement: In a diversity case, the burden of proof on a state-law claim element or defense follows the substantive state right into federal court; federal procedural rules do not override that allocation.
trigger: diversity suit on a state-law claim, plaintiff invokes federal procedural rule to override a state burden allocation
authority: Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938); Guaranty Trust Co. v. York, 326 U.S. 99 (1945)

statement: When a call asks which burden applies to a specific claim element in a diversity case, test each answer against the specific element and the specific body of law, not against abstract labels about burdens in general.
trigger: four short procedural-posture labels in a diversity case; one is the state-burden answer

statement: A Rule 50(b) motion renews, rather than invents, a Rule 50(a) legal-sufficiency challenge; the post-verdict motion is limited to grounds fairly raised in the pre-verdict Rule 50(a) motion.
trigger: defendant files a Rule 50(b) motion on a new ground not raised in the pre-verdict Rule 50(a) motion
authority: Unitherm Food Systems, Inc. v. Swift-Eckrich, Inc., 546 U.S. 394, 404 (2006); Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 50(b)

statement: When the call asks whether the court may grant a renewed Rule 50(b) motion on a new ground, test the new ground against the pre-verdict 50(a) record, not against the doctrinal strength of the new ground.
trigger: four answer choices that each name a different procedural theory (unlimited preservation, importance priority, plaintiff-only availability, correct preservation)

statement: A crossclaim runs against a co-party; a counterclaim runs against an opposing party. Co-defendants on the same side of the caption are co-parties, so the labeled claim between them is a crossclaim under FRCP 13(g).
trigger: one defendant asserts a claim against a co-defendant in the same suit
authority: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 13(a), 13(g)

statement: When the second defendant is already named in the caption, do not reach for impleader — impleader exists precisely to pull a *non-party* in.
trigger: defendant names a non-plaintiff, but the non-plaintiff is already a co-defendant

statement: Rule 12(h)(2) preserves the Rule 12(b)(6) failure-to-state-a-claim defense for any later pleading, motion, or at trial — including a Rule 12(c) motion for judgment on the pleadings after the pleadings close.
trigger: defendant answers without 12(b)(6) and later moves for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 12(c)
authority: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(h)(2)

statement: When the call is 'is the defense waived by omission,' map the precise defense to the precise Rule 12(h) subsection before saying 'waived.' Rule 12(h)(1) waives 12(b)(2)–(5) and 12(b)(7); Rule 12(h)(2) preserves 12(b)(6) and a small list of other defenses; Rule 12(h)(3) addresses 12(b)(1) (subject-matter jurisdiction), which is never waived.
trigger: defendant omits a Rule 12(b) defense from the answer; call is whether the defense is preserved

statement: A natural person's state citizenship for diversity purposes is the state of domicile, defined as physical presence coupled with intent to remain indefinitely. A fixed-term temporary stay does not change domicile; a person keeps her existing domicile until she acquires a new one in a different state.
trigger: person with clear permanent-home state + fixed-term temporary stay in another state + clear intent to return

statement: When the call is 'for diversity purposes, what is her citizenship,' translate the question to 'where is her domicile' and test the two-element definition (physical presence + intent to remain indefinitely) before picking.
trigger: call asks for state citizenship in a diversity-jurisdiction fact pattern

statement: Adequacy of representation is a separate Rule 23(a) prong, distinct from typicality and from the named plaintiff's personal injury. The named plaintiff and class counsel must fairly protect the interests of absent class members; that is a separate inquiry the court must find in addition to numerosity, commonality, and typicality.
trigger: defendant argues that the court must analyze whether the named plaintiff and class counsel can fairly protect absent class members; call is which statement best describes the certification inquiry
authority: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(a)(4)

statement: When the call is 'which statement best describes the certification inquiry,' count the prongs. Rule 23(a) has four: numerosity, commonality, typicality, adequacy. All four must be found. Rule 23(b) further requires one of three categories.
trigger: open-ended 'which statement best describes the certification inquiry' call

statement: The preclusion law that governs a federal-court judgment tracks the source of the substantive claim that produced the judgment: federal-question judgments get federal common-law preclusion; state-law judgments get the preclusion law of the rendering state.
trigger: prior judgment was a federal-question judgment; second action is also federal; call asks which preclusion law governs
authority: Semtek International Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp., 531 U.S. 497 (2001)

statement: When the call asks which preclusion law governs the earlier judgment, ask first: what was the source of the prior judgment — federal question or state law? Then match: federal question → federal common law; state law → rendering state preclusion law. The Erie posture of either case is a separate question.
trigger: call asks 'which preclusion law governs the earlier judgment'

statement: For a state-court judgment, the source of preclusion law is the rendering state under 28 U.S.C. § 1738 and Semtek; federal common law of preclusion controls only federal-court judgments.
trigger: prior judgment is state-court; second court is federal (or vice versa)
authority: 28 U.S.C. § 1738; Semtek International Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp., 531 U.S. 497 (2001)

statement: A single plaintiff may aggregate all claims — related or unrelated — against a single defendant to meet the amount-in-controversy requirement under 28 U.S.C. § 1332; the 'unrelated' qualifier is a red herring when one plaintiff sues one defendant.
trigger: stem describes a single plaintiff suing a single defendant on multiple claims in federal court

statement: When the movant knew of the case from day 1, run the Rule 24 timeliness factors first; the public-importance choice is a misstatement of the mandatory-intervention rule (Rule 24(a)(2) requires impairment of a legally protected interest, not a general public concern).
trigger: movant knew of the case from the start; the proposed intervention would reopen discovery and delay trial; the 'intervention is required' framing is on the table

statement: A federal diversity court must apply the forum state's choice-of-law rules (Klaxon) to determine whether a contractual choice-of-law clause is enforceable, even when the contract names the chosen state's law. The contract clause is not self-executing.
trigger: federal diversity case with a contractual choice-of-law clause naming a non-forum state
authority: Klaxon Co. v. Stentor Electric Mfg. Co., 313 U.S. 487 (1941); Erie R.R. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938); 28 U.S.C. § 1652; Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws § 187(2)

statement: When the call asks how a federal court should decide a choice-of-law question in diversity, the test is the forum-state choice-of-law rules, not the contract's choice-of-law clause, not federal common law, and not party preference.
trigger: federal diversity case involving a contractual choice-of-law clause

statement: Mandamus is an extraordinary writ. It requires the petitioner to show a clear and indisputable right to the relief sought AND the absence of any adequate alternative means of relief. The writ is not a substitute for an appeal; ordinary legal error in denying a routine motion does not clear the standard.
trigger: ordinary interlocutory ruling; defendant seeks mandamus on weak grounds (expense, likely error)
authority: All Writs Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1651(a); Roche v. Evaporated Milk Ass'n, 319 U.S. 21, 26 (1943); Bankers Life & Casualty Co. v. Holland, 346 U.S. 379 (1953)

statement: When the call asks whether mandamus is available for an ordinary interlocutory ruling, run the 'clear and indisputable right' check first. Ordinary legal error in denying a routine motion does not clear the bar; the eventual final-judgment appeal is an adequate alternative means.
trigger: stem describes an ordinary interlocutory ruling and a defendant seeking mandamus on weak grounds

statement: A corporation is a citizen of BOTH its state of incorporation AND the state of its principal place of business (nerve center) for purposes of 28 U.S.C. § 1332. The plaintiff and the corporation cannot both be citizens of the same state for complete diversity to be present.
trigger: corporate defendant with dual-citizenship structure; plaintiff shares one of the corporate citizenships
authority: 28 U.S.C. § 1332(c)(1); Hertz Corp. v. Friend, 559 U.S. 77 (2010)

statement: When the call asks whether complete diversity is present, run the dual-citizenship check on the corporate defendant first. If the corporation's nerve center is in the plaintiff's home state, diversity is destroyed — regardless of the state of incorporation.
trigger: stem describes a corporate defendant with a dual-citizenship structure and a plaintiff sharing one of the corporate citizenships

statement: Under the legal-certainty test, a federal court will not dismiss for lack of amount in controversy unless it appears to a legal certainty that the plaintiff cannot recover more than the statutory threshold. A defendant's prediction that discovery will reduce actual recovery is a factual probability, not a legal bar.
trigger: diverse parties, good-faith pleading above the threshold, defendant argues discovery will show lower damages, no statute or contract caps recovery below the threshold
authority: St. Paul Mercury Indemnity Co. v. Red Cab Co., 303 U.S. 283 (1938); 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)

statement: A defendant's contention that the plaintiff's damages are lower than pleaded does not itself defeat the amount in controversy. Contested damages go to the merits, not to subject-matter jurisdiction.
trigger: defendant's motion to dismiss asserts that discovery will show lower damages (or otherwise disputes the pleaded amount)

statement: Rule 15(c) party-change relation back requires both timely notice within the Rule 4(m) period and a shown Rule 15(c) identity mistake; a John Doe pleading plus a lack of identified defendant is not, by itself, the required mistake.
trigger: John Doe pleading + no service within Rule 4(m) + post-limitations identification + Rule 15(c) motion
authority: Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(c)(1)(C); 1991 amendment Advisory Committee Notes

statement: Read the call to the named party (here, the real driver), then cut the 'yes' overclaims and the immutability overclaim before reaching for a doctrine label.
trigger: John Doe pleading + post-limitations identification + Rule 15(c) motion

statement: Under Erie, a federal diversity court applies state substantive law. The survival of a state-created claim is a substantive question for Erie purposes, so the forum state's survival statute — including a no-survival rule — governs.
trigger: state-law plaintiff dies during federal diversity litigation; forum-state survival statute says the claim does not survive
authority: Erie R.R. Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938); Klaxon Co. v. Stentor Electric Manufacturing Co., 313 U.S. 487 (1941); Wheeling Steel Corp. v. Fox, 298 U.S. 193 (1936)

statement: When the call asks 'what should the federal court do?' in a diversity case involving a state-law claim, the answer is the Erie command, not a merits-preference or diversity-impact analysis.
trigger: federal court, diversity jurisdiction, state-law claim, plaintiff dies during litigation

statement: Rule 23(b)(2) is the natural fit when a class claim targets a single defendant for a single uniform policy or course of conduct and seeks a single injunctive or declaratory remedy that would provide classwide relief — no predominance, no superiority, no opt-out.
trigger: When the stem has one defendant, one uniform conduct, one injunctive remedy, and no individualized damages, ask 'is this a Rule 23(b)(2) case?' first, before defaulting to Rule 23(b)(3).
authority: Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23(b)(2); Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 338 (2011) (cohesion test for Rule 23(b)(2) classes).

statement: When a Rule 23 call has a 1-1-1-0 pattern (one defendant + one uniform conduct + one injunctive remedy + no individualized damages), default to Rule 23(b)(2) before reaching for Rule 23(b)(3). The 1-1-1-0 pattern is the textbook Rule 23(b)(2) shape.
trigger: A class claim with one defendant, one conduct, one injunction, no damages.

statement: Under Hanna v. Plumer, the first step in any Erie analysis is to ask whether a valid Federal Rule of Civil Procedure or valid federal statute directly controls the issue; if it does, the federal directive applies, and the outcome-determinative test does not come into play.
trigger: When the stem names a specific Federal Rule directly on point (e.g., FRE 801 hearsay), lock the federal-directive threshold first; do not reach for the outcome test.
authority: Hanna v. Plumer, 380 U.S. 460 (1965); Erie Railroad Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938); cf. Guaranty Trust Co. v. York, 326 U.S. 99 (1945); Byrd v. Blue Ridge Rural Electric Cooperative, 356 U.S. 525 (1958); Rules Enabling Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2072.

statement: When the stem names a specific Federal Rule directly on point, lock the federal-directive threshold first; do not reach for the outcome test.
trigger: A diversity case with a Federal Rule directly on point.

statement: When the call asks 'what is the appellate route' for a non-final order, scan for a permission-based statute or rule (Rule 23(f), 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b), mandamus, collateral order). The default is no interlocutory appeal as of right.
trigger: defendant files an immediate notice of appeal from a non-final class-certification order and argues that the importance of the question entitles it to appeal as of right

statement: False imprisonment requires intentional confinement. A complaint that pleads only negligent confinement defeats that claim at the motion-to-dismiss stage.
trigger: Complaint labels false imprisonment but says the confinement happened negligently.
authority: Restatement (Second) of Torts §35; Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6); Ashcroft v. Iqbal.

statement: Amount in controversy is not a likely-verdict test. The pleaded amount controls unless it is legally certain the claim is below the jurisdictional threshold.
trigger: Answer choice talks about unlikely recovery above $75,000.
authority: 28 U.S.C. §1332; St. Paul Mercury Indem. Co. v. Red Cab Co.

statement: On a motion-to-dismiss array, match the reason to the motion. Same outcome plus wrong procedural reason is a trap.
trigger: Two choices talk about amount in controversy while one choice talks about failure to state a claim.

statement: Collateral-order review is narrow. Ordinary discovery orders generally wait for final judgment; expense alone is not effective unreviewability.
trigger: Immediate appeal from a discovery order under the collateral order doctrine.
authority: 28 U.S.C. §1291; Cohen; Mohawk; Cunningham.

statement: In an appealability array, sort answers as review-now or review-later. Cut the extreme words first, then ask whether final judgment review is enough.
trigger: Immediate appeal + discovery order + collateral order doctrine.

statement: Attorney-client privilege protects confidential legal-advice communications, not the underlying facts. A fact does not become privileged just because the client told it to a lawyer.
trigger: The discovery request asks for a fact, but the refusal says the fact was told to counsel.
authority: Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383 (1981); Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(1); Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(a)(2).

statement: Before reading privilege choices, name the object of discovery. If the other side asks for the fact itself, do not let an answer switch you to the lawyer conversation.
trigger: Interrogatory asks for an identity or event fact; objection says the fact was told to counsel.

statement: Rule 54(b) is not automatic. A partial judgment in a multi-claim or multi-party civil action is immediately appealable only if the district court directs entry of judgment and determines that there is no just reason for delay.
trigger: Fewer than all claims or parties resolved; claims remain; order lacks certification language.
authority: Fed. R. Civ. P. 54(b).

statement: When the stem goes out of its way to say the order lacks formal Rule 54(b) language, do not let a partial-dismissal fact do the work by itself.
trigger: One party is out, but other claims remain and formal certification is missing.

statement: For immediate appeal, an order can count as an injunction by practical effect. A command to do or stop doing something may be injunctive even when the caption uses another label.
trigger: Non-injunction caption plus a command to stop conduct until trial.
authority: 28 U.S.C. §1292(a)(1); Carson v. American Brands; Abbott v. Perez.

statement: In a label-vs-function appealability question, read the verb in the order before reading the caption. A stop-command is the navigation signal.
trigger: Order caption says one thing; operative sentence commands a party not to act.

statement: In a diversity case, a defendant's same-transaction counterclaim can use supplemental jurisdiction even below $75,000 unless a specific plaintiff-side §1367(b) bar applies.
trigger: Defendant counterclaim + same incident + no independent amount in controversy.

statement: Read the array as result plus jurisdictional reason. A 'yes' answer is not enough; the reason must be same-event supplemental jurisdiction, not federal question.
trigger: A counterclaim in a diversity case with no independent amount.

statement: When a valid federal statute directly controls a federal-court procedural issue, apply the federal statute before Erie twin-aims balancing.
trigger: Diversity case + state procedural rule + federal statute on point.
authority: 28 U.S.C. § 1391; Hanna v. Plumer; Stewart Organization v. Ricoh.

statement: On a 'which rule controls' call, do not pick the rule that creates the preferred outcome. First identify whether a federal statute directly answers the procedural question.
trigger: Answer choices compare state rule, federal statute, and forum-shopping policy.

statement: For ordinary federal civil actions, venue can sit in the event district or in a defendant-residence district when all defendants reside in that same state; the plaintiff's home is not a venue bucket.
trigger: The call asks which judicial districts are proper and gives accident location plus defendants from different districts of one state.

statement: Read list answers as bucket checklists: keep every valid bucket and reject any answer that adds a false bucket or omits a true one.
trigger: Choices mix event district, defendant districts, and plaintiff home district.

statement: For ordinary diversity jurisdiction, citizenship is measured when the complaint is filed. A later move does not create diversity that was missing at filing.
trigger: A stem gives citizenship at filing and a later domicile change.
authority: 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a); Grupo Dataflux v. Atlas Global Group, L.P.; Mollan v. Torrance

statement: When a jurisdiction stem gives filing-day citizenship and later domicile facts, freeze the snapshot at filing before judging the later facts.
trigger: same-state parties at filing plus a later move before answer or trial

statement: Personal jurisdiction is a waivable Rule 12(b)(2) defense. If it was available and the defendant omitted it from the first answer or first Rule 12 motion, it is waived.
trigger: A defendant answers or files a Rule 12 motion without objecting to personal jurisdiction.

statement: An amended complaint does not automatically revive a Rule 12(b)(2)-(5) defense that was available and waived earlier unless the amendment first creates the defense.
trigger: Plaintiff amends after defendant already failed to raise a known threshold defense.
authority: Gilmore v. Shearson/American Express, Inc.; State Auto Ins. Co. v. Thomas Landscaping & Constr., Inc.; Gnotec Reftele AB order.

statement: Match the jurisdiction word to the call before doing doctrine. Personal jurisdiction is defendant-court power; supplemental jurisdiction is subject-matter power over claims.
trigger: A choice switches from personal jurisdiction to supplemental jurisdiction.

statement: Specific jurisdiction starts with defendant-created forum contacts. Fairness or convenience can defeat jurisdiction after contacts exist, but it cannot create contacts by itself.
trigger: The plaintiff felt harm at home or argues the home forum is fair, while the defendant's conduct all occurred elsewhere.
authority: International Shoe; World-Wide Volkswagen; Walden; Ford.

statement: In a specific-jurisdiction array, sort contacts first and fairness second. A plaintiff-side hardship fact cannot do the work of a defendant-side contact fact.
trigger: Choices mention hardship, injury felt in the forum, and no forum-directed defendant conduct.

statement: Forum property is not a magic key. If the claim is unrelated to the attached property, the forum still needs a defendant-forum-litigation connection.
trigger: A plaintiff attaches a defendant's forum property to sue on an unrelated personal claim.
authority: Shaffer v. Heitner, 433 U.S. 186; International Shoe Co. v. Washington, 326 U.S. 310.

statement: Separate court power from collection. An asset's value may matter after a valid judgment, but it does not answer whether this court can decide the claim.
trigger: An answer asks whether the attached property can satisfy the whole judgment.
